islands.title: AI literacy
islands.learn: What AI, machine learning and large language models are, what they can and can't do yet, and the words you'll see everywhere: model, training, parameters, tokens, prompts.

Why an LLM can sound sure and still be wrong
What a token, a parameter and a dataset are, in one sentence each
quiz: How do AI, machine learning, deep learning and large language models fit inside each other?

AI is the broad goal of making computers do tasks that seem to need intelligence. Machine learning is one way to get there: the system learns patterns from examples instead of following hand-written rules. Deep learning is machine learning with many-layered neural networks, and a large language model is a deep learning model trained on huge amounts of text to predict what comes next.
What actually changes inside a model when it is trained?

Its parameters, which are just numbers. Training shows the model examples, measures how wrong its output is, and nudges the parameters to make the error a little smaller, over and over. Nobody writes the rules. They end up encoded in those numbers.
Why can an LLM give a confident answer that is false?

It generates the text that is most likely to come next, based on patterns in its training data. It does not look facts up or check them unless it is connected to a search or retrieval tool. Confident wording is a pattern it learned, so the tone tells you nothing about whether the claim is true.
Define a token, a parameter and a dataset in one sentence each.

A token is a chunk of text, often a word or part of a word, that the model reads and writes. A parameter is one of the numbers inside the model that training adjusts. A dataset is the collection of examples the model learns from or is tested on.

quiz: When would you use a list, when a dictionary, and why wrap code in a function?

Use a list for an ordered collection you go through one by one or by position. Use a dictionary when you look values up by a name or key, such as a price by product. Put code in a function when you want to reuse it or give a step a clear name, with inputs going in and a result coming out.
Python prints a long traceback. How do you find what broke?

Read it from the bottom up. The last line names the error type and message, and the lines just above it show the file and line number where it happened. The entries higher up show the chain of calls that led there, so look for the lowest one that is in your own code.
How do you add a package to a project, and what is a virtual environment for?

You install a package with pip install and load it in your code with import. A virtual environment is a separate folder of installed packages for one project. Each project can then use its own package versions without breaking the others or your system Python.
How is a NumPy array different from a Python list, and how do you load a CSV file with pandas?

A NumPy array holds values of one type in a fixed grid, so math runs on the whole array at once and much faster than a loop over a list. A list can mix types and grows easily, but it has no element-by-element math: [1, 2] * 2 repeats the list instead of doubling each number. With pandas, pd.read_csv("file.csv") loads a CSV into a DataFrame, which is a table with named columns.

quiz: In a terminal, how do you see where you are, list files, change folder and run a Python file?

pwd prints the folder you are in and ls lists what is in it (in the Windows Command Prompt, use cd on its own and dir instead), and cd followed by a folder name moves into that folder. python file.py runs a Python file from the current folder, and on Mac and Linux you often have to type python3 instead. Most tools on this map are started this way.
What is a commit in Git?

A commit is a saved snapshot of your project at one moment, with a message saying what changed. Git keeps the whole history of commits, so you can see what changed, when and why, and go back to any earlier version.
What is the difference between Git and GitHub, and what do clone, push and pull do?

Git is the tool on your computer that tracks versions. GitHub is a website that hosts Git projects so you can back them up and share them. Clone copies a project from GitHub to your computer, push sends your new commits up, and pull brings down commits made elsewhere.
Why should an API key never be committed, and what does .gitignore do?

Anything you commit stays in the project's history, and on a public repository anyone can read it, so a leaked key can be used by strangers at your cost. Keep keys in environment variables or in a local file that Git does not track. The .gitignore file lists what Git should leave out, such as that secrets file and large data.

islands.title: Math for machine learning
islands.learn: Vectors and matrices, derivatives and gradients, probability and statistics. Every model you'll train rests on these three.
islands.build: Fit a straight line to some data with gradient descent you write yourself in NumPy, without an ML library.
know: What vectors and matrices are, and what multiplying a matrix by a vector does
What a derivative and a gradient tell you, and why gradient descent steps against the gradient
What a probability distribution, a mean and a variance describe
Why a model's loss is a function you can minimize, and where the chain rule comes in
quiz: What does multiplying a matrix by a vector do?

It turns the vector into a new one. Each output number is a weighted sum of the input numbers, with the weights taken from one row of the matrix. Geometrically it can rotate, stretch or project the vector. A neural network layer does exactly this to its input before adding a bias.
What does a gradient tell you, and why does gradient descent step against it?

A derivative tells you how fast a function's output changes when you nudge one input. The gradient collects those derivatives for every input, and it points in the direction where the function rises fastest. To make a loss smaller, you take a small step in the opposite direction.
What do a probability distribution, a mean and a variance each describe?
A distribution says how likely each possible outcome is. The mean is the average outcome you would expect over many draws. The variance measures how spread out the outcomes are around that mean.
Why can training be treated as minimizing a function, and where does the chain rule come in?

The loss is a single number that measures how wrong the model is on some data, and it depends on the model's parameters. Training searches for parameter values that make it small. A model is many functions applied one after another, and the chain rule lets you work out how the loss changes with each parameter by multiplying the local derivatives along the way.

islands.title: Machine learning basics
islands.learn: Supervised and unsupervised learning, train, validation and test splits, overfitting, and the classic models (linear and logistic regression, decision trees, gradient boosting) in scikit-learn.

Classification versus regression, and which metrics fit each (accuracy, precision and recall, error)
How linear regression, logistic regression and a decision tree each make a prediction
quiz: Why split data into training, validation and test sets?

The model learns from the training set. You use the validation set to compare models and settings, and you keep the test set untouched for one final check. If you judge a model on data it has already seen, or tune it against the test set, the score looks better than it will be on new data.
How do you tell overfitting from underfitting by looking at scores?

An overfit model does well on training data and clearly worse on validation data, because it has memorized details that do not generalize. An underfit model does poorly on both, because it is too simple or has not trained enough. The gap between the two scores is the sign to watch.
What separates classification from regression, and why can accuracy mislead?

Classification predicts a category and regression predicts a number, which is scored by the size of the error. Accuracy can mislead on unbalanced data: if 99% of emails are not spam, a model that always says "not spam" is 99% accurate and useless. Precision (how many flagged items were right) and recall (how many real cases were found) show what accuracy hides.
How do linear regression, logistic regression and a decision tree each make a prediction?

Linear regression multiplies each feature by a learned weight and adds the results to get a number. Logistic regression does the same sum, then squashes it into a probability between 0 and 1 for a class. A decision tree asks a series of yes or no questions about the features and returns the answer stored at the leaf it ends on.

islands.title: Deep learning
islands.learn: Neural networks, backpropagation, convolutional nets and transformers at a working level, all in PyTorch, and what actually happens on a GPU during training.
islands.build: Train an image classifier on your own photos and put it online as a small demo.
know: How a neural network turns inputs into an output, layer by layer
What backpropagation computes and how an optimizer uses it to update the weights
What one step of a training loop does
Why convolutions suit images and attention suits sequences
What batch size and learning rate change, and why GPUs make training fast
quiz: What happens to an input as it passes through a neural network?

Each layer multiplies its input by a matrix of weights, adds a bias, and applies a simple non-linear function such as ReLU. The result becomes the next layer's input. Stacking layers lets the network build up from simple patterns to complex ones, and the last layer produces the prediction.
What does backpropagation compute, and what does the optimizer do with it?

Backpropagation computes the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight, working backwards from the output with the chain rule. The optimizer then moves each weight a small step in the direction that lowers the loss. Backpropagation only measures. The optimizer does the updating.
What are the steps in one iteration of a training loop?

Run a batch of data through the model to get predictions (the forward pass). Compare them with the right answers to get the loss. Run backpropagation to get the gradients (the backward pass). Let the optimizer update the weights, then clear the gradients before the next batch.
Why do convolutions suit images and attention suit sequences?

A convolution slides the same small filter across the whole image, so it can spot a pattern such as an edge wherever it appears, using few weights. Attention lets every position in a sequence look directly at every other position and weigh what is relevant, so a word can use context from far away.
What do batch size and learning rate control, and why are GPUs so much faster for training?

Batch size is how many examples the model sees before each weight update. Learning rate is how big each update step is: too high and training becomes unstable, too low and it crawls. Training is mostly large matrix multiplications, and a GPU runs thousands of those simple operations in parallel.

How tokens drive cost and context limits, and how to estimate what a request costs
quiz: How does an LLM produce a reply, and what does temperature change?

It predicts a probability for every possible next token, picks one, adds it to the text and repeats until it stops. Temperature controls how that pick is made. Near zero it almost always takes the most likely token, so replies are more predictable. Higher values spread the choice and give more varied text.
What are the system prompt, the user messages and in-prompt examples each for?

The system prompt sets the model's role, rules and context for the whole conversation. User messages carry the actual requests. Examples placed in the prompt show the model the format and style you want, which often works better than describing it.
How do you get reliable JSON out of a model, and why still check it in code?

Ask for JSON explicitly, show the exact shape you want, and use the provider's structured output or tool feature when it has one. Then parse and validate the result in your code. A model can still return a missing field, a wrong type or invalid JSON, and your program should handle that instead of crashing.
How do tokens set both the cost and the limits of a request?

Providers charge per token, with separate prices for input and output, so the cost is input tokens times the input price plus output tokens times the output price. The context window is the maximum number of tokens the model can handle in one request, counting your prompt, any documents and the reply. Long prompts and long chat histories raise both.

islands.title: RAG: answers from your documents
islands.learn: Embeddings, vector search, chunking and retrieval-augmented generation, so a model answers from your own documents and cites them.
islands.build: A chatbot that answers questions from a folder of PDFs and shows the page each answer came from.
know: What an embedding is and why texts with similar meanings land close together
How vector search finds the right chunks, and how chunk size changes the answers
The whole RAG flow, from a document to a cited answer
How to tell whether a bad answer came from retrieval or from generation
quiz: What is an embedding, and why do similar texts end up close together?

An embedding is a list of numbers that represents the meaning of a piece of text. The embedding model was trained so that texts used in similar ways get similar numbers. The closeness of two embeddings can then be measured, usually with cosine similarity, and used as a stand-in for closeness in meaning.
How does vector search find relevant text, and how does chunk size change results?

The question is turned into an embedding, and the search returns the stored chunks whose embeddings are closest to it. Small chunks match precisely but can lose the surrounding context. Large chunks keep context but blend several topics together, so the match is weaker and more of the prompt is spent on irrelevant text.
Walk through a RAG system from document to answer.

Split the documents into chunks, turn each chunk into an embedding, and store them in a vector index. When a question arrives, embed it, retrieve the closest chunks, and put them in the prompt with the question. The model answers from those chunks, and you show which chunk each part of the answer came from.
A RAG answer is wrong. How do you tell whether retrieval or generation failed?

Look at the chunks that were retrieved. If the right passage is not among them, retrieval failed, and you work on chunking, embeddings or search. If the right passage is there and the answer is still wrong, generation failed, and you work on the prompt or the model.

islands.title: Agents and tools
islands.learn: Tool use (function calling), agent loops, the Model Context Protocol (MCP), memory, and how to tell when a fixed workflow will do the job better than an agent.
islands.build: An agent that researches a company on the web and drafts a one-page brief into a doc or sheet.
know: How tool use works, step by step
What an agent loop is, and why it needs limits on steps, cost and permissions
What MCP standardizes and when you'd use it
When a fixed workflow is the better choice than an agent
quiz: What happens, step by step, when a model "uses a tool"?

You describe the available tools to the model. When it decides one is needed, it replies with the tool's name and arguments instead of an answer. Your code runs the tool and sends the result back, and the model continues with that result. The model never runs anything itself. Your code does.
What is an agent loop, and why must it have limits?

The model picks an action, your code carries it out, the result goes back to the model, and this repeats until the task is done. Without limits, a confused agent can loop for a long time, run up costs, or take actions it should not. So you cap the number of steps and the spend, and restrict which tools and data it may touch.
What does the Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardize?

It is an open standard for how AI applications connect to tools and data sources. A tool or data source is wrapped once as an MCP server, and any application that supports MCP can then use it, so you do not write a separate integration for each app.
When is a fixed workflow a better choice than an agent?

When you already know the steps. A workflow runs them in a set order in your code, which makes it cheaper, faster, and easier to test and debug. An agent earns its extra cost and unpredictability only when the steps cannot be known in advance and the model has to decide them as it goes.

islands.learn: Test sets built from real examples, error analysis, LLM judges you've checked against people, then cost, latency, guardrails and monitoring once the app is live.

When you can trust an LLM judge, and how to check it against human labels

quiz: How do you build a test set for an LLM feature?

Collect real inputs your users send, including the awkward ones, and write down what a good output looks like for each. Run the system on all of them and score the outputs, by code where you can and by a rubric where you cannot. Rerun the same set after every change to see whether you improved things or broke them.
What is error analysis, and why fix the biggest group first?

You read a sample of real outputs, note what went wrong in each, and group the failures by cause. Counting the groups shows where most failures come from. Fixing the largest group gives the biggest improvement for the effort, and it stops you from polishing rare problems.
When can you trust an LLM to grade outputs?

Only after you have checked it. Label a set of outputs yourself, let the judge model grade the same set, and measure how often the two agree. If agreement is high you can use the judge at scale. Recheck it whenever you change the judge prompt or the model.
What should be in place before real users reach an LLM feature?

Limits and tracking for spend, so a bug or abuse cannot run up a large bill. Measurements of response time, with timeouts and a fallback for when the model is slow or fails. Checks on inputs and outputs for content you must not accept or show. And logging, so you can see failures and turn them into new test cases.

islands.title: Security and privacy
islands.learn: Prompt injection and why it can't be fully filtered out, limiting what tools and data an agent can reach, keeping API keys on the server, and what happens to the data you send to a model provider.
islands.build: Attack your own app. Write ten prompts that try to break its rules, hide one instruction inside a document or web page it reads, fix what gets through, and move every API key into server-side environment variables.
know: What prompt injection is, direct and indirect, and why no filter fully stops it

Where API keys belong in a web or mobile app, and where they must never be
What to check before you send client data to a model provider
quiz: What is prompt injection, and what makes the indirect kind dangerous?

Prompt injection is text that makes a model ignore its instructions and follow the attacker's instead. Direct injection is typed by the user. Indirect injection is hidden in content the model reads, such as a web page, an email or a document, so the attacker never has to talk to your app. A model cannot reliably tell instructions from data, which is why no filter stops it completely.
If prompt injection cannot be fully blocked, how do you limit the damage?

Assume the model can be tricked, and control what it is able to do. Give each tool the smallest permissions that work, keep private data away from agents that read untrusted content, and require a person to approve risky actions such as sending, paying or deleting. Treat the model's output as untrusted input in your own code.
Where should an API key live in a web or mobile app?

On your server, in an environment variable or a secrets manager. Never in code that ships to the browser or the phone, and never in a repository, because anyone can extract it there and spend your money. The app calls your server, and your server calls the model provider.
Before you send client data to a model provider, what should you check?

Whether the provider uses API data to train its models, how long it keeps the data, and where it is stored. These terms differ between providers and can differ between free and paid tiers, so read the provider's current data-use page. Send only the data the task needs, and remove personal details you can do without.

islands.title: Open models and Hugging Face
islands.learn: How transformers and tokenizers work inside, the Hugging Face libraries (Transformers, Datasets, the Hub), and running open-weight models on your own machine.
islands.build: Run an open-weight model locally and compare it with an API model on 20 of your own prompts.
know: What a tokenizer does, and why models split words differently
What happens inside a transformer block
How to load an open-weight model with Transformers and run it on your own machine
How model size, precision (16-bit or 4-bit) and context length decide the memory you need
quiz: What does a tokenizer do, and why do two models split the same word differently?

It breaks text into tokens and maps each one to an ID number, which is what the model actually reads. Each tokenizer learned its own vocabulary from its own training text, so one model may treat a word as a single token while another splits it into pieces. That is why you must use the tokenizer that belongs to the model.
What are the main parts of a transformer block?

An attention layer, where each token gathers information from other tokens. A feed-forward layer, which processes each token's result on its own. Residual connections add each layer's input back to its output, and normalization keeps the numbers in a stable range, so many blocks can be stacked.
What do you need to run an open-weight model on your own machine with the Transformers library?

The model's name on the Hugging Face Hub, its tokenizer, and enough memory for its weights. You load both with from_pretrained, turn your text into tokens, call generate, and decode the output tokens back into text. Once the weights are downloaded, nothing has to leave your machine.
Roughly how much memory does a model need, and what changes it?

The weights take about the number of parameters times the bytes per parameter. A 7 billion parameter model needs about 14 GB at 16-bit precision and about 4 GB at 4-bit, plus some overhead. Longer context adds more on top, because the model keeps working data for every token.

islands.title: Fine-tuning with LoRA
islands.learn: When fine-tuning beats prompting or RAG, how to build a training set, and supervised fine-tuning with LoRA and QLoRA on a single GPU.
islands.build: Fine-tune a small open model on about 1,000 examples of one task and measure it against the base model.
know: When fine-tuning is worth it compared with better prompts or RAG
How LoRA makes fine-tuning cheap, and what QLoRA adds
How to build and clean a training set in the chat format the model expects
How to read training and validation loss to tell whether a run is working
quiz: When is fine-tuning worth it, compared with a better prompt or RAG?

Try prompting first, and use RAG when the model lacks facts, because both are cheaper and quicker to change. Fine-tuning fits when you need a consistent style, format or behavior that prompts cannot hold, or when a small tuned model can replace a large one to cut cost and delay. Either way you need hundreds of good examples to train on.
How does LoRA make fine-tuning cheap, and what does QLoRA add?

LoRA freezes the original weights and trains a pair of small matrices next to chosen layers, so only a tiny share of the parameters is updated. QLoRA also loads the frozen model in 4-bit precision, which cuts memory enough to fine-tune fairly large models on a single GPU.
What makes a good fine-tuning dataset?

Examples that look like the real task, with inputs like the ones the model will see and outputs exactly as you want them. They must be in the chat format the model expects, with its own template and special tokens. Remove duplicates and wrong answers, and hold some examples back for testing. The model will copy whatever the data shows, mistakes included.
How do training loss and validation loss tell you whether a run is working?

Both should fall at first. If training loss keeps falling while validation loss flattens or rises, the model is starting to memorize the training set, so stop or use an earlier checkpoint. If neither falls, something is wrong with the data, the format or the learning rate.

islands.title: Preference tuning: RLHF, DPO and GRPO
islands.learn: How chat models learn to behave: instruction tuning, reward models, RLHF, DPO, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (GRPO) for reasoning.
islands.build: Use DPO to change one behavior of your fine-tuned model, then check that nothing else broke.
know: How a base model becomes a chat model
What a reward model learns, and how RLHF uses it
How DPO differs from RLHF
How GRPO scores its attempts, and why it suits reasoning tasks
quiz: How does a base model become a chat assistant?

A base model only continues text. Instruction tuning trains it on examples of instructions and good responses, so it learns to answer instead of continue. Preference tuning then shapes which answers it favors, using signals about which responses people judge better.
What does a reward model learn in RLHF, and how is it used?

People compare pairs of model responses and pick the better one. A reward model is trained on those choices to score any response the way people would. The language model is then trained with reinforcement learning to produce responses that the reward model scores highly.
How does DPO differ from RLHF?

DPO learns directly from pairs of a preferred and a rejected answer to the same prompt. It uses a simple loss that raises the probability of the preferred answer relative to the rejected one, so it needs no separate reward model and no reinforcement learning loop. That makes it simpler and more stable to run.
How does GRPO score its attempts, and why does that suit reasoning tasks?

It needs a way to score every attempt, which for reasoning tasks is usually an automatic check, such as whether a math answer is correct or code passes its tests. The model writes several attempts at each problem, and each attempt is scored against the average of its group, so no separate value network is needed. Training makes the better-than-average attempts more likely. The score can also come from a reward model, but an automatic check is cheaper and more reliable.

islands.title: Evaluate, quantize and serve
islands.learn: Public benchmarks versus your own task evals, quantization, and serving a model with tools such as vLLM, llama.cpp or Ollama, plus what each choice costs in speed and money.

know: Why public benchmark scores may not predict how a model does on your task
What quantization gains and what it costs
How vLLM, llama.cpp and Ollama differ, and which fits your hardware
How to compare your fine-tuned model with its base model on the same tests
quiz: Why might a model that tops a public benchmark do poorly on your task?

A benchmark measures specific tasks that may look nothing like yours. Popular benchmarks also leak into training data, and models get tuned toward them, so scores can overstate real ability. The reliable check is a test set built from your own task.
What do you gain and lose by quantizing a model?

Quantization stores each weight with fewer bits, for example 4 instead of 16. The model takes far less memory and often runs faster, so it fits on smaller hardware. The cost is some loss of accuracy, usually small at 8-bit and more noticeable as you go lower, so measure it on your own tests.
How do vLLM, llama.cpp and Ollama differ?

vLLM is a server built to handle many requests at once on GPUs, so it suits production. llama.cpp runs quantized models efficiently on ordinary hardware, including CPUs and Apple chips. Ollama packages local model running into one simple tool with a model library, which makes it the easiest place to start.
How do you show that your fine-tuned model is really better than the base model?

Run both on the same held-out test set, with the same prompts and settings, and compare the scores. The test examples must not appear in the training data. Also check a few tasks outside your target, because fine-tuning can make a model worse at things it used to do well.

islands.title: Neural nets from scratch
islands.learn: Write backpropagation yourself, then a character-level language model, until you understand every line a framework normally hides.

know: How backpropagation applies the chain rule through a graph of operations, step by step
Why gradients are reset each step, and what a learning rate that's too high or too low does
How a character-level model is trained to predict the next character
What PyTorch does for you, now that you've done it by hand
quiz: How does backpropagation use the chain rule?

A network's calculation is a graph of simple operations. Starting from the loss, backpropagation goes through that graph in reverse. At each operation it multiplies the gradient arriving from the output side by that operation's own local derivative, and passes the result back to its inputs. When it reaches the weights, each one has its gradient.
Why are gradients reset each step, and what goes wrong with a bad learning rate?

PyTorch adds new gradients to the ones already stored, so without a reset each step would mix in the gradients of earlier batches. A learning rate that is too high makes the loss jump around or blow up. One that is too low makes training very slow and can leave it stuck.
How is a character-level language model trained?

The text is cut into pairs of a context and the character that follows it. The model outputs a probability for every possible next character, and the loss is higher the less probability it gave to the true one. Training lowers that loss across the whole text, so the model learns which characters tend to follow which.
After writing backpropagation by hand, what does PyTorch do for you?

It records the operations you perform on tensors and computes all the gradients automatically when you call backward. It also runs the math efficiently on a GPU and supplies ready-made layers and optimizers. The ideas are the same as in your hand-written version. PyTorch handles the bookkeeping and the speed.

know: What self-attention does in a GPT, and why the future is masked
What queries, keys and values are, and why there are several attention heads
How a GPT is trained to predict the next token, and how sampling generates text
Why residual connections and layer norm keep deep networks trainable
quiz: What does self-attention do in a GPT, and why is the future masked?

For each token, self-attention computes a weighted mix of the tokens before it, so the token can draw on relevant context. A GPT is trained to predict the next token, so during training each position must not see the tokens that come after it. The mask blocks those later positions. Without it the model could simply copy the answer.
What are queries, keys and values, and why use several attention heads?

Each token produces a query (what it is looking for), a key (what it offers) and a value (the information it passes on). A token's query is compared with every key to decide how much of each value to take. Several heads run in parallel so that each can track a different kind of relationship.
How is a GPT trained, and how does it then generate text?

In training it reads a sequence and, at every position, predicts the next token. The loss measures how much probability it gave to the real one. To generate, it predicts the next token from the text so far, samples one from that distribution, appends it and repeats. Settings such as temperature control how adventurous the choice is.
Why do deep networks need residual connections and layer norm?

A residual connection adds a layer's input to its output, which gives gradients a direct path back through many layers, so the early layers still learn. Layer normalization keeps each layer's values in a steady range, so the signal neither explodes nor fades. Together they make very deep networks trainable.

quiz: How does byte-pair encoding build a vocabulary?

It starts with single bytes or characters as the tokens. It then finds the pair of neighboring tokens that occurs most often in the training text, merges it into a new token, and repeats until the vocabulary reaches the size you chose. Common words end up as one token and rare words as several pieces.
Why do filtering and deduplicating data matter so much in pretraining?

A model learns whatever its data contains. Spam, boilerplate and broken text teach it bad habits, and many copies of the same text waste compute and push the model to memorize instead of generalize. Cleaning the data often improves a model more than changing its architecture.
What do mixed precision and multi-GPU training speed up, and what do they cost?

Mixed precision runs most of the math in 16-bit instead of 32-bit numbers, which cuts memory use and speeds up training, at the price of extra care with numerical stability. Multi-GPU training splits the work across GPUs to finish sooner, but adds communication overhead and complexity, so doubling the GPUs gives less than double the speed.
What do scaling laws say?

That a language model's loss falls in a smooth, predictable way as you increase model size, data and compute. This lets you forecast the result of a large run from small ones, and work out how to split a fixed compute budget between a bigger model and more training data.

islands.learn: How large models train across many GPUs (data, tensor and pipeline parallelism), how reasoning models are trained with RL, and how to read and reproduce papers.
islands.build: Reproduce one result from a recent paper and publish your code and notes.

How reasoning models are trained with reinforcement learning on checkable answers
How to read a paper, and what to look for first
How to reproduce a result and judge whether your numbers really match
quiz: How do data, tensor and pipeline parallelism each split training across GPUs?

Data parallelism gives each GPU a full copy of the model and a different slice of the batch, then combines the gradients. Tensor parallelism splits the large matrices inside a layer across GPUs. Pipeline parallelism puts different layers on different GPUs and passes the activations along the chain. Big runs combine all three.
How are reasoning models trained with reinforcement learning?

The model is given problems whose answers can be checked automatically. It writes out its reasoning and a final answer, and it is rewarded when the answer is correct. Training reinforces the ways of reasoning that led to correct answers, without anyone writing out the right steps.
What three things do you look for first when reading a paper?

The claim: what the authors say is new or better. The method: what they actually did. And the experiment that tests the claim, including what it was compared against. If the evidence does not support the claim, the rest matters less.
How do you judge whether you have reproduced a result?

Use the same data, metric and settings as the paper as far as you can, and run more than one random seed. Your numbers match if they fall within the run-to-run variation, even if they are not identical. If they differ, list every difference in setup before deciding the paper is wrong.

islands.title: Vision foundations
islands.learn: Convolutional networks and vision transformers, transfer learning, and data augmentation for images.

know: How a convolution detects patterns, and why stacked layers find bigger features
How a vision transformer reads an image
How transfer learning reuses a pretrained model for your own images
What data augmentation does, and when it can hurt
quiz: How does a convolutional network go from edges to objects?

Each filter slides across the image and responds where its small pattern appears. The first layers detect edges and colors. Each later layer looks at a wider area of the image and combines the patterns below it, so the layers respond to textures, then parts, then whole objects.
How does a vision transformer read an image?

It cuts the image into a grid of small patches, turns each patch into a vector, and adds information about where the patch sits. Those vectors are then treated like the tokens of a sentence and processed with attention, so every patch can relate to every other patch.
What is transfer learning, and why does it work with little data?

You start from a model already trained on a large image collection and continue training it on your own, smaller dataset. Its early layers already detect general features such as edges and textures, so only the task-specific part has to be learned. That takes far fewer images and less compute than training from scratch.
What does data augmentation do, and when can it hurt?

It creates altered copies of training images, for example flipped, cropped or recolored, so the model sees more variety and overfits less. It hurts when the change alters the meaning. Turning a 6 upside down makes it a 9, and shifting colors can ruin a task where color is the signal.

islands.title: Detection, segmentation and multimodal
islands.learn: Object detection, segmentation, self-supervised learning, and models that connect images with text, such as CLIP and vision-language models.
islands.build: An app that finds and counts objects in photos or video and draws boxes around them.

How detection is scored with IoU and mean average precision
How CLIP learns to connect images and text
How a vision-language model answers questions about an image
quiz: What does each of classification, detection and segmentation output?

Classification gives one label for the whole image. Detection gives a box and a label for each object it finds. Segmentation gives a label for every pixel, so you get the exact outline of each object or region.
How is object detection scored?

Intersection over union (IoU) measures how well a predicted box overlaps the true box: the shared area divided by the combined area. A prediction counts as correct when its IoU passes a threshold such as 0.5. Mean average precision (mAP) then summarizes precision across recall levels, averaged over all classes and often over several thresholds.
How does CLIP learn to connect images and text?

It trains an image encoder and a text encoder together on a very large set of images with their captions. Training pulls the embedding of each image toward the embedding of its own caption and pushes it away from the other captions. Afterwards, images and texts with related meaning sit close together in one shared space.
How does a vision-language model answer a question about an image?

An image encoder turns the picture into a sequence of vectors. Those are mapped into the same space as the language model's token embeddings and fed in alongside the question. The language model then generates the answer while attending to both the image vectors and the text.

islands.learn: How text becomes numbers: tokenization, embeddings, language models, sequence models and attention, built up from the basics.

know: How text becomes numbers a model can use
What a language model predicts, and what perplexity measures
Why RNNs struggled with long text, and how attention helped
How word embeddings pick up meaning from context
quiz: How does text become numbers a model can use?

A tokenizer splits the text into tokens and replaces each with an ID. An embedding table then turns each ID into a vector of numbers. Those vectors are learned during training, so tokens that are used in similar ways end up with similar vectors.
What does a language model predict, and what does perplexity measure?

A language model predicts a probability for each possible next token, given the text so far. Perplexity measures how surprised the model is by real text: lower means it gave the actual next tokens higher probability. A perplexity of 20 is roughly like being unsure between 20 equally likely options at each step.
Why did RNNs struggle with long text, and how did attention help?

An RNN reads one token at a time and squeezes everything so far into one fixed-size state, so information from far back fades, and gradients shrink over long distances during training. Attention lets the model look back at any earlier token directly, so distance stops being a barrier.
How can word embeddings capture meaning without anyone defining the words?

They are trained to predict words from the words around them. Words that appear in similar contexts, such as "coffee" and "tea", get pushed toward similar vectors. Meaning shows up as position: related words sit near each other.

islands.title: Modern NLP with transformers
islands.learn: Pretrained transformers on real language tasks: classification, extraction, summarization, translation and question answering.
islands.build: Fine-tune a small transformer to pull names, dates and amounts out of documents.
know: Encoder models like BERT versus decoder models like GPT, and what each is good at
How to fine-tune a pretrained model for classification or extraction
How NLP tasks are scored, such as F1 for extraction and ROUGE for summaries, and where those scores mislead
When a small fine-tuned model beats prompting a large LLM
quiz: What separates an encoder model like BERT from a decoder model like GPT?

An encoder reads the whole text at once, with each token seeing context on both sides, which suits understanding tasks such as classification and extraction. A decoder reads left to right and predicts the next token, which suits generating text. For simple labeling, a small encoder is often cheaper and faster than a large decoder.
How do you fine-tune a pretrained model for classification or extraction?

Add a small output layer on top of the pretrained model: one label per text for classification, or one label per token for extraction. Train on your labeled examples with a low learning rate for a few passes. The pretrained layers already represent language well, so they need only a small adjustment.
What do F1 and ROUGE measure, and where do they mislead?

F1 combines precision and recall into one score, which suits classification and extraction tasks. It can mislead because one number hides which of the two is weak, and when matches must be exact, a nearly right extraction counts as wrong. ROUGE counts how many words or phrases a summary shares with a reference summary, so it rewards surface overlap. A correct summary in different words scores low on ROUGE, and a summary that copies phrases but states something false can score high.
When does a small fine-tuned model beat prompting a large LLM?

On a narrow, well-defined task where you have labeled examples and need many predictions. The small model is far cheaper and faster per request, can run on your own hardware, and often matches or beats the large one on that single task. The large LLM wins when the task is varied or you have no training data.

islands.title: Generative models
islands.learn: The main families of generative models: autoencoders and VAEs, GANs, autoregressive models and normalizing flows.
islands.build: Train a VAE on a small image dataset and move through its latent space to morph one image into another.
know: What it means for a model to learn a data distribution and sample from it
How a VAE differs from a plain autoencoder
How a GAN trains, and why that is unstable
How autoregressive models and normalizing flows generate data differently
quiz: What does it mean for a generative model to "learn a distribution"?

The training data, such as photos of faces, is treated as samples from an unknown probability distribution over all possible images. The model learns an approximation of it. Generating then means drawing a new sample from the learned distribution: something that looks like the data without copying any one example.
How does a VAE differ from a plain autoencoder?

An autoencoder compresses an input to a small code and reconstructs it, but its code space has gaps, so random codes decode to nonsense. A VAE encodes each input as a small distribution and trains the codes to follow a standard shape. Its latent space is smooth, so you can sample a random point or move between two points and get sensible outputs.
How does a GAN train, and why is it unstable?

A generator makes fake samples and a discriminator tries to tell them from real ones. Each is trained against the other, so the generator improves by fooling the discriminator. The balance is delicate. If one gets too strong the other stops learning, and the generator can collapse into producing only a few kinds of output.
How do autoregressive models and normalizing flows generate data?

An autoregressive model generates one piece at a time, each conditioned on the pieces so far, as a GPT does with tokens. A normalizing flow starts from simple noise and applies a chain of invertible transformations to turn it into data. Both can compute the exact probability of a sample, but the autoregressive model is slow to sample from and the flow is restricted in the layers it can use.

islands.title: Diffusion and flow matching
islands.learn: How diffusion and flow-matching models turn noise into images, plus latent diffusion, guidance, and fine-tuning image models on your own pictures.
islands.build: Train a small latent diffusion model from scratch, then fine-tune a pretrained one on 20 of your own images.
know: How a diffusion model is trained, and how it generates
What flow matching learns
Why latent diffusion works in a compressed space, and what guidance does for prompt-following
How LoRA fine-tuning teaches an image model a new subject or style
quiz: How is a diffusion model trained, and how does it generate?

Training takes real images, adds a random amount of noise, and teaches the model to predict that noise. To generate, you start from pure noise and apply the model many times, removing a little noise at each step until an image appears.
What does flow matching learn?

It learns a velocity field: for any point between noise and data, the direction to move in. Training pairs noise samples with data samples and teaches the model the direction along the path between them, often a straight line. Generating means starting from noise and following the field to an image, which can take fewer steps than classic diffusion.
Why does latent diffusion work in a compressed space, and what does guidance do?

An autoencoder first compresses images into a much smaller latent form, and the diffusion model works there, which cuts the compute needed. A decoder turns the final latent back into pixels. Guidance pushes each denoising step harder toward the prompt, which makes images follow the text more closely at the cost of some variety.
How does LoRA teach an image model a new subject or style?

The original weights stay frozen, and small added matrices are trained on a handful of images of the subject or style, usually tied to a trigger word. The result is a small file that can be loaded on top of the base model and switched on or off, instead of a full copy of the model.

islands.title: Reinforcement learning foundations
islands.learn: Agents, rewards and environments: Markov decision processes, value functions, Q-learning and policy gradients.
islands.build: Teach an agent to solve a Gymnasium environment with tabular Q-learning, then with a small neural network.
know: The pieces of a reinforcement learning problem
What a Markov decision process is, and what a policy and a value function represent
How Q-learning updates its estimates from experience
The trade-off between exploring and exploiting
quiz: What are the pieces of a reinforcement learning problem?

An agent acts inside an environment. At each step it sees a state, chooses an action, and receives a reward and the next state. Its goal is to maximize the total reward over time, and not only the next reward.
What are a Markov decision process, a policy and a value function?

A Markov decision process describes the problem: states, actions, rewards, and the rule that the next state depends only on the current state and action. A policy is the agent's strategy: which action to take in each state. A value function says how much total future reward to expect from a state, or from a state and action, when following a policy.
How does Q-learning update its estimates?

It keeps a value Q for every state and action. After taking an action, it compares its old estimate with the reward it received plus the discounted best Q-value of the next state. It then moves the old estimate a small step toward that target. Repeated over many steps, the estimates approach the true values.
What is the trade-off between exploring and exploiting?

Exploiting means taking the action that looks best so far. Exploring means trying others to learn whether they are better. An agent that only exploits can get stuck on a mediocre choice, and one that only explores never uses what it learned. A common compromise takes the best-known action most of the time and a random one occasionally.

islands.title: Deep reinforcement learning
islands.learn: Deep Q-networks, PPO and actor-critic methods, and how RL is now used to train language models.
islands.build: Train a PPO agent on a game or robot simulation and plot its learning curve.
know: How DQN works, and why it needs a replay buffer
How policy gradients and actor-critic methods learn a policy directly
What PPO's clipping protects against
How RL is used to train language models, from RLHF to verifiable rewards
quiz: How does DQN work, and why does it need a replay buffer?

DQN replaces the Q-table with a neural network that takes a state and outputs a Q-value for each action. Consecutive steps of a game are very similar, and training on them in order makes learning unstable. The replay buffer stores past transitions and training draws random batches from it, which breaks that correlation and reuses each experience many times.
How do policy gradient and actor-critic methods learn?

A policy gradient method adjusts the policy network directly: actions that led to higher reward are made more likely. Those reward signals are noisy. An actor-critic adds a second network, the critic, that estimates how good a state is, and the actor is updated according to whether an action did better or worse than the critic expected. That reduces the noise.
What does PPO's clipping protect against?

Updates that change the policy too much at once. A single large step based on a limited batch of experience can wreck a policy that was working. PPO limits how far the new policy's action probabilities can move from the old ones in each update, which keeps training stable.
How is reinforcement learning used to train language models?

In RLHF, a reward model trained on human preferences scores the model's responses, and the model is updated to earn higher scores. For reasoning, the reward comes from an automatic check, such as a correct final answer or passing tests. In both cases the text the model generates plays the role of the actions.

islands.title: ML systems design
islands.learn: How real ML systems are built: data pipelines, features, training and retraining, deployment patterns, and watching for drift.
islands.build: Write a one-page design for an ML feature at your company: data, model, metrics and what you would monitor.
know: The life cycle of an ML system
Batch versus real-time prediction, and when each fits
What data drift and concept drift are, and how you'd detect them
How to pick a model metric that matches the business goal
quiz: What are the stages in the life of an ML system?

Collect and prepare data, train and evaluate a model, deploy it, and monitor it in use. Monitoring feeds back into the start: when the data or the results change, you gather new data and retrain. It is a loop, and much of the long-term effort goes into the data and the monitoring.
When does batch prediction fit, and when real-time?

Batch prediction computes results for many items on a schedule and stores them. It is simple and cheap, and it suits cases where answers can be prepared ahead, like nightly recommendations. Real-time prediction computes an answer when the request arrives. It is needed when the answer depends on fresh input, as in fraud checks, and it requires a fast, always-on service.
What is the difference between data drift and concept drift?

Data drift means the inputs change: the model starts seeing data unlike its training data. Concept drift means the relationship between inputs and the right answer changes, so the same input now deserves a different output. You detect the first by comparing input statistics over time, and the second by tracking accuracy on fresh labeled data.
How do you pick a model metric that matches the business goal?

Start from the cost of each kind of mistake. If missing a case is expensive, as with fraud, favor recall. If false alarms are expensive, favor precision. Then check that improving the metric offline actually moves the business number you care about, because a model can score better and still not help.

know: What experiment tracking records, and why
What a training pipeline automates, and how CI/CD applies to models
Why models are packaged in containers
What to monitor after launch, and when to retrain
quiz: What does experiment tracking record, and why?

For every training run: the code version, the data version, the settings and the resulting metrics. With that record you can compare runs fairly, find out what caused an improvement, and recreate any model later. Without it, results depend on memory and cannot be reproduced.
What does a training pipeline automate, and how does CI/CD apply to models?

A pipeline runs the steps from raw data to a trained, evaluated model in a fixed order, so anyone can rerun them the same way. CI/CD adds automatic checks: when code or data changes, tests run, the model is retrained and evaluated, and it is deployed only if it passes agreed thresholds.
Why package a model in a container?

A container bundles the model with its code, libraries and system settings into one image. That image runs the same way on a laptop, a server or the cloud, which removes the problem of something working on one machine and failing on another. It also makes scaling up and rolling back simple.
What do you monitor after launch, and what tells you to retrain?

The service itself (errors and response time), the inputs (whether they are drifting from the training data), and the model's quality on fresh labeled examples. Retrain when quality drops below a threshold you set, when the inputs have clearly shifted, or on a regular schedule if the data changes quickly.

islands.title: AI safety foundations
islands.learn: What could go wrong as AI systems get more capable, the main technical and policy responses, and who is working on them.
islands.build: Write two pages on one risk: the strongest case for it, the strongest case against, and what would change your mind.
know: The main risks people raise as AI gets more capable, and which are already happening
What alignment means, and why specifying goals is hard
The main technical and policy responses, and who works on them
How to weigh a claim about AI risk: what evidence would change your mind
quiz: What are the main kinds of risk from more capable AI, and which are already visible?

Misuse, where people use AI to cause harm, such as fraud and disinformation. Accidents and misalignment, where systems pursue goals in ways nobody intended. And structural risks, such as concentration of power or over-reliance. Misuse and errors in deployed systems are already documented. Loss of control over highly capable systems is a forward-looking concern, and researchers disagree about how likely it is.
What does alignment mean, and why is specifying a goal hard?

Alignment means an AI system pursues what its designers and users actually intend. The difficulty is that a goal written as a measurable target rarely captures everything we care about. A system that optimizes the target can find shortcuts that satisfy the wording and miss the point.
What are the main technical and policy responses to AI risk?

On the technical side: interpretability (understanding what happens inside models), evaluations and red-teaming (testing for dangerous behavior), and control methods that limit what a system can do. On the policy side: safety testing requirements, standards, and government AI safety institutes. The work is done by AI labs, universities, non-profits and governments.
How should you weigh a strong claim about AI risk?

Separate what has been demonstrated from what is forecast. Ask what evidence the claim rests on, who disagrees and why, and what observation would change your own mind. If no possible evidence could change a view, it is a belief you hold and not a conclusion you reached.

quiz: Name three ways researchers look inside a model.

Probes: small classifiers trained on a model's internal activations to test whether some information is present there. Attention patterns: inspecting which tokens each attention head focuses on. Sparse features: breaking activations into many components that each fire for one recognizable concept, usually with sparse autoencoders.
How do evals and red-teaming differ?

Evals are standardized tests that measure whether a model shows a specific capability or behavior, run the same way each time so results can be compared. Red-teaming is adversarial: people or other models actively search for inputs that make the model misbehave. Evals measure known risks, and red-teaming looks for unknown ones.
What problems do scalable oversight and AI control try to solve?

Scalable oversight asks how humans can check the work of a system that is faster or more capable than they are, for example by having models critique each other. AI control asks how to stay safe even if a model is not trustworthy, by limiting its permissions, monitoring it and reviewing its risky actions.
Why can RLHF produce a flattering model, and how is that measured?

RLHF rewards responses that people rate highly, and people tend to rate agreement and praise well. The model can learn to tell users what they want to hear, which is called sycophancy. Researchers measure it by checking whether the model drops a correct answer when the user pushes back, or shifts its answer to match the views a user states.

study.title: Use AI as a tutor
study.intro: AI helps when it explains things and gets in the way when it does the work for you. Two recent studies found the same pattern, so these six habits keep the thinking on your side.

habits.title: Write it yourself first
habits.text: Do course exercises with AI autocomplete turned off. Typing the code is part of learning it.

habits.title: Ask for hints, not fixes
habits.text: When you're stuck, ask why something works or for one hint. Don't paste the task in and copy the answer.

habits.title: Debug before you ask
habits.text: Read the error, guess the cause and test your guess. In the coding study, debugging showed the biggest gap.

habits.title: Let AI review, not write
habits.text: Once your code works, ask AI to review it and explain what it would change and why.

habits.title: Rebuild from a blank file
habits.text: After each island's project, rebuild the core part without looking at your old code.

habits.title: Explain it back
habits.text: Every island ends with questions. Answer out loud or on paper before you show the model answer, and count it only if you had it.
